title: Nine Pots on a Windowsill. A Slow Experiment in Growing Something
body: It started with a basil plant from the supermarket, the kind sold to die, squeezed into a plastic pot like a commuter. I repotted it out of pity and it lived, and the living of it turned into nine pots on a south-facing windowsill and the closest thing I have to a semester course in patience. The nine pots hold basil, mint, two pots of parsley that never forgave me, rosemary, a chili plant of aggressive opinions, and three pots of seeds currently negotiating with the soil. The casualty list from last year includes two basils drowned with love, one rosemary lost to a heat wave while I was away, and a mint that died of the opposite, a week of forgotten water, proving that plants do not want your devotion. They want your consistency, a distinction I have failed to learn in several other departments of life. The first real lesson the windowsill taught is the speed of feedback. In most of my work, the gap between action and result is weeks, sometimes quarters, and the gap is where bad habits go to hide. In the pots, the gap is days. Overwater on Tuesday, yellow on Friday. Move the pot ten centimeters on Sunday, lean by Wednesday. The plants run the tightest feedback loop in my life, and I have started to notice they are training me, not the reverse. I water more gently now. I watch before I act. Nine pots is a small number of pots and a large number of remedial lessons. The second lesson is about partial control, which the pots teach with a firmness no app has managed. I control the water, the soil, the pot size, the position. The plant controls everything else. The chili grew toward the glass all summer, crooked, producing exactly four chilis, each one a small event. I could not make it straight. I could only offer conditions. There is a management seminar somewhere in that sentence, and I have sat through the seminar, and the chili said it better. The daily ritual is two minutes and it has become load-bearing. Morning, look at every pot. Not do, look. The three minutes of looking caught the aphids in week one of their invasion, caught the droop before the wilt, caught the fact that the rosemary pot's drainage had failed, one day before the rosemary would have caught it instead. Two minutes of looking per day is the entire difference between a windowsill garden and a windowsill cemetery, and the skill it builds, noticing before intervening, transfers to everything. I catch my own mistakes earlier at work now. The pots got there first. The harvest is honest and small. Basil for the kitchen, mint enough for summer tea, four chilis, the parsley still on strike. Nobody could live on this windowsill. That was never the experiment. The experiment was whether a person with a screen-heavy life could maintain a slow, daily, physical relationship with nine small lives, and the answer, after a year, is yes, with two drownings and a heat wave on the record. The seeds are negotiating. Two pots have said yes, green commas breaking the soil, and the third is thinking about it, and every morning the first thing I do is look, and the looking has taught me the thing the pots were for. Everything alive is slower than my impatience and faster than my despair. The windowsill sits between those two clocks and makes me practice being a person who can keep an appointment with both.
